title: UA Museums celebrate Halloween with event inspired by Hodges Meteorite
excerpt: UA Museums will host “Haunting at the Museums: Otherworldly Encounters” at Smith Hall and the Gorgas House Museum Oct. 27.
content:
Skip to content

TUSCALOOSA, Ala. — University of Alabama Museums will host Haunting at the Museums: Otherworldly Encounters at the Alabama Museum of Natural History and Gorgas House Museum Oct. 27 from 5 to 8 p.m. The free, family-friendly and all-ages event is inspired by a famous meteorite that fell on Sylacauga and will explore the phenomena of specters, space, spirits and science.

The Alabama Museum of Natural History is home to the Hodges Meteorite, which crashed through Ann Hodges’ rooftop, bounced off her Philco radio and struck her in the side. Thankfully, Ann survived the incident, but in 1954, as Cold War tensions were high, the Hodges Meteorite was first believed to be a spy satellite from Russia. This paranoia was at its peak merely a few years before the Hodges’ Philco radio was manufactured in 1941.

On Halloween 1938, Orson Welles directed and narrated an infamous radio episode titled “War of the Worlds” based on H.G. Wells’ novel of the same name. This one drama was so convincing that listeners were fully convinced that Martians were attacking Earth. With the out-of-this-world renovation of the Hodges Meteorite exhibit at the Alabama Museum of Natural History, Haunting at the Museums decided to beam back to 1938. 

“We invite you to join us for an evening of extraterrestrial exploration through hands-on activities provided by our community partners,” said Kristin Harrell, education outreach coordinator at the Alabama Museum of Natural History. “We will delve into the discoveries and the debunking of phenomena of extreme encounters, creatures, and out-of-this-world experiences.”

At the Gorgas House Museum, visitors can see the Halloween exhibit, Calling the Spirits In: Spiritualism in America, to learn about tools of the trade, celebrities who worked to both promote and debunk the practice, and how mass casualties on both sides of the Civil War led to a new religious movement.

Guests at the Gorgas House Museum can also hear stories about the ghosts of the Gorgas family who still walk the halls.

While admission to the Alabama Museum of Natural History and the Gorgas House Museum is free between 5 and 8 p.m., donations are welcome and appreciated. Costumes and period-appropriate clothing are welcome but not required.

For more information on these events, visit the UA Museums website.
